cues.text: Could a big multiplication be hiding three smaller facts? Let's investigate!
Our goal is to use place value to make multiplying easier.
For three hundred and twenty-four times eight, we can split the number into three hundred, twenty and four.
Which part would you try first? Keep your prediction in mind.
Here's the useful discovery: multiply each part by eight, then combine the results. Every part matters!
You have turned one big question into familiar facts. What a helpful strategy to explain to a friend!
